newsitem.title: JAPAN: East Asia Gold - Prices seen weak but demand rising.
newsitem.headline: East Asia Gold - Prices seen weak but demand rising.

text.p: Gold prices are likely to come under further pressure after news Australia's central bank had sold a large amount of its reserves, but lower prices could generate demand in some East Asian countries, traders and analysts said on Friday.
The Reserve Bank of Australia announced early on Friday it had sold 167 tonnes -- more than two thirds of its holdings -- of its gold reserves in the past six months.
The sales by Australia, a major gold producer, triggered concern about central banks' attitude towards gold and fears that other central banks may follow suit, traders said.
"Australia's decision suggested that the attractiveness of gold as an asset, which bears no interest rates, is fading," a Tokyo-based industry analyst said.
Taiwan's central bank said on Friday it had no plan to sell gold at the moment.
"We have had some internal review of how we might change our gold reserve policy," said Hsu Chia-tung, Taiwan central bank vice governor. "But right now this cannot be implemented."
Despite reassurance from the central bank, Taiwan traders were nevertheless concerned about potential sales by other central banks.
"The Australian central bank's new gold reserve policy may start another round of government selling," a gold trader at Taiwan's China Trust Bank said.
Gold slumped to a 12-year low in New York on Thursday following the news of the Australian central bank's sales.
Prices are expected to be in for another battering, traders said.

"Foreign bullion traders told us gold prices would fall to $280 to $300 an ounce this year. Some traders are expecting the price could fall to $250 an ounce," a dealer with another South Korean trading house said.
Taiwan traders said the global gold prices could test support at $320 an ounce in the near-term.
"Gold is still very bearish," a gold dealer at Pan Asia Bank said. "It may test $320 soon."
In late Friday Asian trade, bullion stood at $324.00/325.00 per ounce.
Cheaper gold prices, however, may stimulate physical gold demand in some from Asian countries, traditional bargain hunters, like Taiwan and South Korea, traders said.
In South Korea, domestic demand for imported gold was seen rising as prices neared those of smuggled gold, bullion dealers in Seoul said on Friday.

"Gold demand by domestic wholesalers is picked up this morning as imported gold prices are nearly the same as those of smuggled gold due to the sharp price fall (overnight) in New York," a dealer with a major trading house said.
But other dealers said growth in domestic demand could be limited due to an economic slowdown following a series of corporate collapses in the country.
In Taiwan, gold demand from individual buyers and the jewellery industry has increased sharply as a result of the recent weakness in world gold prices, dealers said.

Traders estimated Taiwan's gold demand from the jewellery industry has risen about 20 percent since late June, while investor buying has jumped by about 50 percent in the past five days alone, a dealer at Taiwan's Central Trust of China said.
"Individual buyers' gold demand increased about 50 percent this week," the dealer at Central Trust said. "Industrial demand is up by about 20 percent."
Taiwan traders said gold prices had been bearish due to periodic sales of gold by European central banks since last year, which were aimed at easing budget deficits.
Belgium in March 1996, confirmed a 203 tonne sale. -- Contributed by Taipei, Seoul Newsrooms
